class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Signals are sums of harmonics.",
            "Average value is the constant term.",
            "Coefficients represent weights of frequencies.",
            "Adding waves sharpens the shape.",

        ]
        self.setup_layout("The Core Formula: Breaking it Down", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Signals are sums of harmonics.
        formula = MathTex(
            "f(t) = \\frac{a_0}{2} + \\sum_{n=1}^{\\infty} \\left[ a_n \\cos(n\\omega t) + b_n \\sin(n\\omega t) \\right]",
            font_size=32
        )
        # Fix for Issue 26, 28, 37: Update placement for formula to avoid clutter and overlap
        self.place_in_area(formula, 'B2', 'C4', scale_factor=0.5)
        self.play(Write(formula))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFFFFF")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Average value is the constant term.
        a0_box = SurroundingRectangle(formula[0][4:8], color="#FFFF00")
        self.play(Create(a0_box))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFFF00")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Coefficients represent weights of frequencies.
        an_box = SurroundingRectangle(formula[0][17:19], color="#FF00FF")
        bn_box = SurroundingRectangle(formula[0][27:29], color="#00FFFF")
        self.play(Create(an_box), Create(bn_box))
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FF00FF")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # Adding waves sharpens the shape.
        axes = Axes(x_range=[0, 2*PI, 1], y_range=[-2, 2, 1], axis_config={"include_tip": False}, x_length=4, y_length=2)
        # Fix for Issue 27, 37: Updated placement for axes
        self.place_at_grid(axes, 'D3', scale_factor=0.7)
        
        # Simple square wave approximation demo
        wave = axes.plot(lambda t: 4/PI * (np.sin(t)), color=WHITE)
        self.play(Create(axes), Create(wave))
        self.lecture[3].set_color("#00FF00")
        self.wait(1)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        # Complexity emerges from simple components.
        wave_sharp = axes.plot(lambda t: 4/PI * (np.sin(t) + np.sin(3*t)/3), color="#00FF00")
        self.play(Transform(wave, wave_sharp))
        self.lecture[4].set_color("#FF8800")
        self.wait(2)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Compression discards low-weight frequencies.",
            "Noise removal filters chaotic signals.",
            "Fourier analysis empowers modern technology.",
            "Chaotic waves become clear data.",
            "Mathematics cleans our digital world."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Real-World Application: Compression and Noise", lecture_lines)
        
        # Assets
        microphone = SVGMobject("/scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/microphone.svg")
        computer = SVGMobject("/scratch/pawsey1357/jthen/Code2Video/assets/icon/computer.svg")

        # Placement in columns 4-6 as per B004
        self.place_at_grid(microphone, "C5", scale_factor=0.5)
        self.add(microphone)
        self.place_at_grid(computer, "D5", scale_factor=0.5)
        self.add(computer)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Show a complex, jagged signal waveform (#FF0000)
        t = np.linspace(0, 4 * np.pi, 200)
        y = np.sin(t) + 0.3 * np.sin(20 * t) + 0.1 * np.random.normal(0, 0.5, 200)
        complex_signal = VMobject(color="#FF0000")
        complex_signal.set_points_smoothly([np.array([t[i] * 0.2, y[i] * 0.3, 0]) for i in range(len(t))])
        
        # Positioning: Column 4-6, Rows D-F as per B004, B019, Critic feedback (D1-F6 or similar)
        self.place_in_area(complex_signal, 'D4', 'F6', scale_factor=0.6)
        self.play(Create(complex_signal), self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#FF0000"))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Animate the removal of high-frequency noise components.
        clean_y = np.sin(t)
        clean_signal = VMobject(color="#00FF00")
        clean_signal.set_points_smoothly([np.array([t[i] * 0.2, clean_y[i] * 0.3, 0]) for i in range(len(t))])
        clean_signal.move_to(complex_signal.get_center())
        
        self.play(ReplacementTransform(complex_signal, clean_signal), self.lecture[1].animate.set_color("#00FF00"))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color("#FFFF00"))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[3].animate.set_color("#00FFFF"))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color("#FF00FF"))
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: The Magic of Pure Fourier Series: Decomposing Complexity

sections.title: The Hook: The Musical Analogy
sections.content: Introduce the concept that any complex periodic signal is just a 'chord' made of 'pure notes.' Define the Fourier Series as a mathematical way to decompose a complicated wave into simple sine and cosine components.
sections.example: Visualize a grand piano playing a single chord. The Fourier Series acts like a 'mathematical prism' that splits that chord into its individual, pure frequency notes.

sections.title: Prerequisite: Orthogonality of Sine/Cosine
sections.content: Briefly explain the 'Basis' concept. Just as 3D space uses x, y, and z axes, periodic functions use a set of sine/cosine functions as an orthogonal basis. This allows us to measure 'how much' of each frequency exists in the signal.
sections.example: Imagine trying to describe a position on a map using only North-South and East-West lines. If these lines weren't perpendicular, it would be messy. Sine/cosine functions are the perfect 'grid' for periodic signals.

sections.title: The Core Formula: Breaking it Down
sections.content: Present the summation formula: f(t) = a₀/2 + Σ[aₙ cos(nωt) + bₙ sin(nωt)]. Explain that a₀ is the average, and aₙ/bₙ are the 'weights' or amplitudes for each harmonic frequency.
sections.example: An animation showing a square wave gradually forming as we add more sine waves (n=1, n=3, n=5...). Each wave added makes the shape sharper and more defined.

sections.title: Calculating the Ingredients: Euler-Fourier Coefficients
sections.content: Explain how to find the 'weights' (aₙ and bₙ) using integration over one period. Emphasize that these integrals represent the correlation between the target signal and the reference frequency.
sections.example: A visual 'slider' interface where you change the frequency (n). As you slide through values, the graph shows the signal 'filtering' in or out, like tuning an old-fashioned radio.

sections.title: Real-World Application: Compression and Noise
sections.content: Conclude by showing how this theory powers modern technology. By identifying and discarding the 'low-weight' frequencies, we can compress files or clean up noisy data.
sections.example: Show a digital audio signal from a robotic dog. The raw signal looks like chaotic static, but the Fourier Series highlights a single 'barking frequency' (the signal) vs the background static (noise) that can be easily removed.
